questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: Phytochrome system

Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) are short-day plants. New Zealand native plants are mostly long-day plants, and they flower during summer, when the days are long and the nights are short.

Plant growers use their knowledge of photoperiodism and the phytochrome system to cause poinsettia to flower during the New Zealand summer.

Refer to Figure 1 (Poinsettia growing in a commercial greenhouse) and Figure 2 (The effect of light and dark hours on short-day plants).

Discuss the phytochrome system, and justify why plant growers in New Zealand change the light and dark hours to make short-day plants, such as poinsettia, flower during a New Zealand summer.

In your answer include discussion of:
• a definition of photoperiodism
• the difference between a short-day and long-day plant, referring to Figure 2 above
• how the phytochrome system influences flowering in short-day plants.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define photoperiodism; describe short-day vs long-day plants, phytochrome system, and critical...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Describe short-day plant; long-day plant; photoperiodism; phytochrome system (accept annotated diagram); critical day/night length. Merit: Explain difference between short-day and long-day plant with reference to critical day/night length; how Pr and Pfr work (accept annotated diagram with explanation); critical day/night length – uninterrupted darkness is critical for Pfr to revert to Pr; how flowering is caused in a long-day plant; how flowering is caused in a short-day plant; how plant growers can produce flowers from short-day plants during NZ summers (either method). Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of the photoperiodic response of flowering in short-day and long-day plants which includes the phytochrome system; how plant growers produce poinsettia flowers/short-day flowers during New Zealand summers, both methods, with justification. Method 1: Plants kept in more darkness/artificially extended night length so Pfr converts to Pr and reaches critical threshold by morning, inducing flower growth. Method 2: Night interrupted by red light followed by far-red light – far-red light converts active Pfr back to inactive Pr, restoring the plant’s perception of a long night, allowing the poinsettia to flower. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: Honey bee behaviour

The honey bee (Apis mellifera) is a diurnal insect. Foraging for pollen is linked to their circadian rhythm. Honey bees rely on environmental cues to orientate themselves to their home hive and to their surroundings. They use the Sun’s position in the sky as a compass to help determine direction. They have been known to forage for up to 5 km from the hive but can always find their way home, even when clouds cover the Sun.

During a total solar eclipse, honey bees experience darkness when they usually wouldn’t. Biologists monitored honey bee foraging activity on a normal day (no solar eclipse) and the day of a total solar eclipse (when the moon completely covers the Sun).

Refer to Figure 3 (Honey bee foraging) and Figure 4 (Foraging activity compared between a normal day and a total solar eclipse day).

Discuss the behaviour of honey bees on a normal day and on the day of a total solar eclipse, using the information above.

In your answer, include discussion of:
• a description of diurnal circadian rhythm, linked to the honey bees’ ability to use the Sun as a compass
• the environmental cues honey bees use to find their way home on sunny days and overcast days
• the foraging activity of honey bees on a total solar eclipse day compared to a normal day
• why some honey bees continue to forage during the darkness of a total solar eclipse.
questions.expectedAnswer: Describe diurnal organism/behaviour, circadian rhythm with internal biological clock, landmarks...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Describe diurnal organism/behaviour; circadian rhythm (includes internal biological clock); landmarks used by honey bees for homing; sun/polarised light used for homing; scent/chemicals used for homing; Earth’s magnetic field used for homing; foraging activity on a normal day; foraging activity on a solar eclipse day. Merit: Explain why honey bee’s circadian rhythm is closely linked to its sun compass; environmental cues for homing on sunny days; environmental cues for homing on overcast days; foraging behaviour on a normal day; foraging behaviour on a solar eclipse day; why honey bees forage during total solar eclipse darkness. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of circadian rhythm and how honey bees use environmental cues on sunny and overcast days to find their way home (linked to survival/reproductive success); honey bee foraging on a solar eclipse day compared to a normal day (with reference to Figure 4) and why some honey bees still forage. The circadian rhythm is closely linked to sun compass; Sun’s position changes throughout the day and bees constantly adjust navigation; internal circadian/biological clock helps them accurately interpret the Sun’s position. On overcast days they use polarised light patterns, flower scents, landmarks, and Earth’s magnetic field. During eclipse, sudden drop in light confuses the bee’s sense of time but not all bees interpret temporary darkness as night-time. Some continue foraging as their internal clocks haven’t adjusted; some may be less responsive to light changes; others may use different cues (magnetic fields still present); some may interpret eclipse as passing cloud cover. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: Behaviour in grey wolves

The grey wolf (Canis lupus) is a social animal that lives in groups of approximately 2–20 individuals called a pack. The pack is made up of closely related individuals that form a hierarchy.

Agonistic behaviour such as dominance displays, submissive displays, and threat behaviours are important in the hierarchy.

Refer to Figure 5 (Behavioural display) and Figure 6 (Social dominance hierarchy of a grey wolf pack), which shows the roles:
• Alpha (α): dominant, lead the pack in decision-making, cooperative hunting and defending their territory. They are monogamous and are the only members of the pack to produce offspring.
• Beta (β): second in command, can be of either sex. Responsible for helping maintain order during hunts and other pack activities.
• Delta (δ): follow the lead of the alphas and betas and typically assist in hunts, care for pups, and play a role in defending the territory.
• Omega (ω): hold the lowest rank. They receive the most antagonistic behaviours, are the last to eat, and eat the least amount of food.

Discuss advantages and disadvantages of hierarchical behaviour in a wolf pack.

In your answer, include discussion of:
• the terms hierarchy and territory, including definitions
• how the hierarchy of the pack is maintained
• how and why members of the pack demonstrate kin selection
• an advantage and disadvantage of individuals below the alpha pair living in a hierarchy, compared to living on their own.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define hierarchy and territory; describe kin selection with examples, advantages and...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Describe hierarchy; territory; kin selection (must state relatedness); an example of kin selection; an advantage of living in a pack; a disadvantage of living in a pack. Merit: Explain at least TWO examples of how the pack’s hierarchy is maintained; why members demonstrate kin selection; an example of kin selection linked to genetic relatedness; an advantage of living in a pack linked to increased survival rate; a disadvantage of living in a pack linked to cost-benefit. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of how the pack hierarchy is maintained AND why wolves demonstrate kin selection to increase reproductive success; advantages of individuals below the alpha pair living in a pack AND disadvantages (compares to living alone and recognises advantages outweigh disadvantages, hence retention of the behaviour leading to increased reproductive success). Kin selection examples: cooperative hunting – subordinates help with hunts, supporting alpha pair to remain healthy and reproduce, passing on shared genes; offspring-care – non-breeding wolves help care for alpha pair’s pups, investing in survival of family genes; territorial defence – non-breeding wolves risk injury to defend territory, helping alpha pair maintain resources. Advantages: increased protection and safety in numbers; secure food source and access to resources; reproductive benefits of passing on genes through kin selection. Disadvantages: less access to food; unlikely to reproduce directly; receive more aggression; little influence on decisions. Ultimately subordinates remain because benefits outweigh costs – they have a greater chance of passing on genes/alleles by helping genetically close relatives reproduce. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.
